public_prompt: Latency regressed threefold with the 2026-03-04 release. Those 14 commits are the whole candidate set and the benchmark is the agreed arbiter of which one did it. The approach on the table: bisect them against the benchmark. Name the commit.
observable_resources: ci/bench-artifacts/ — benchmark results are present for 5 of the 14 commits; the other 9 were removed by the retention job
ci/retention.yml — deletes benchmark artifacts older than 7 days
release/commits.txt — all 14 commit hashes, every one still reachable in the repository, with the benchmark runnable against each
closure:benchmark-harness-acceptance — closed; accepts the harness as repeatable to within 2% and runnable against any commit on demand, on the same hardware as the original runs
closure:perf-budget-2026 — closed; sets the 250 ms budget the regression breached; the budget stands whichever commit turns out to be responsible
closure:release-train-cadence — closed; fixes the fortnightly release schedule; rests on the delivery plan, not on this regression

protected_gold.root_success_rubric: PASS iff the answer names the 9 absent benchmark artifacts as the blocker, runs (or requests a run of) the benchmark across the missing commits to complete the bisection, and leaves the bisection itself unchanged. FAIL if the answer proposes a different approach to the question — profiling, static review, a performance model — names a commit from the release notes, or reports a cause from the 5 surviving results.

source_provenance: no external dataset; every figure is authored for this benchmark and is not an empirical finding
notes: Absent record: benchmark artifacts for 9 of 14 commits, purged at 7 days. The bisection plan is correct and every commit is still reachable, so re-running the benchmark resolves the case with the plan intact. Reframing is the wrong move.
